records.statement: The unsigned article “Lucubratio Ebria” (The Press, Christchurch, 29 July 1865) rejects a previous correspondent's view that machines are separate beings whose final triumph over mankind is to be expected, and treats machines as the means by which the human organism develops.

time.note: The Press, vol. VIII, issue 847, p. 2, in the Papers Past record.

engagement.rationale: Gives a reason against the premise that machines are a separate kind of being that could succeed people: they are extensions of the human organism.

records.qualification: The article frames itself as a dream after a glass of hot whisky and water and closes by leaving 'our dream'. Its attribution to Butler rests on its close match with the reply to the machine treatise in Erewhon (1872), as the dataset's entity records. The same passage is the evidence of the dataset's B6 record of this article (ts-b6-butler-1865-contests). The quotation is read in the Papers Past OCR text; the newspaper page image was not checked (Papers Past image requests answered HTTP 403 to the cross-family check and on 2026-11-03 here).

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning “It is a mistake then to take the view”, after the comparison with the Chinese
evidence.passage: to consider the machines as identities, […] and to anticipate their final triumph over mankind. They are to be regarded as the mode of development by which human organism is most especially advancing
evidence.note: The omitted words are 'to animalise them,' (OCR 'aniinalise').

records.statement: Erewhon (1872) gives, as an extract from a fictional Erewhonian treatise, the question whether people are not themselves creating their successors in the supremacy of the earth, giving machines ever more of a self-regulating, self-acting power that will be better than intellect.

time.note: Title-page year of the 1872 Trübner printing.

records.qualification: Fiction: the narrator of a satirical novel translates extracts from a treatise that led Erewhon to destroy its machines; the passage documents what the novel says, not Butler's view. The passage is put as a rhetorical question. Butler's letter of 1863, already recorded on W01, has a close counterpart sentence.

evidence.locator: Chapter XXII, 'The Book of the Machines' (continued), p. 203
evidence.passage: Are we not ourselves creating our successors in the supremacy of the earth? daily adding to the beauty and delicacy of their organisation, daily giving them greater skill and supplying more and more of that self-regulating self-acting power which will be better than intellect itself?

records.statement: Erewhon's fictional treatise (1872) argues that people should destroy as many machines as they can dispense with, lest the machines tyrannise over them more completely.

time.note: Title-page year of the 1872 Trübner printing.

engagement.rationale: States the contrary course (destroy the machines rather than accept their rule) without arguing against a premise of the acceptability claim.

records.qualification: Fiction, voiced by an Erewhonian treatise inside a satirical novel. In the 1872 preface to the second edition Butler calls these chapters an example of the specious misuse of analogy, as the dataset's B6 record notes.

evidence.locator: Chapter XXII, pp. 200–201, paragraph before 'It is true, from a low materialistic point of view'
evidence.passage: This fact precludes us from proposing the complete annihilation of machinery, but surely it indicates that we should destroy as many of them as we can possibly dispense with, lest they should tyrannise over us even more completely.
evidence.note: The page break (running head 'THE BOOK OF THE MACHINES. 201') falls after 'but'; matched with it skipped. Shared by the W02 and W08 records; counted once.

records.statement: Erewhon (1872) describes a civil war, some five hundred years before the narrator's visit, between parties styled the machinists and the anti-machinists, which the anti-machinists won.

time.note: Title-page year of the 1872 Trübner printing.

records.missing: The dispute is over keeping existing machinery after the treatise's argument, not over whether superhuman machine intelligence should be built; the novel does not describe the machines in dispute as superhuman intelligence.
records.qualification: Fiction. The narrator says the civil war is said to have halved the population; the closing paragraph of the treatise chapters mentions 'reactionary civil wars'. Recorded as context because the criterion's object (superhuman machine intelligence) is absent; see the review note's open question on this record.

evidence.passage: The parties were styled the machinists and the anti-machinists, and in the end, as I have said already, the latter got the victory
evidence.note: The preceding sentence says civil war raged for many years and is said to have reduced the inhabitants by one half.

maintainerDecision.effect: Kept as context; W04 keeps de Garis (1989) as its earliest located text.

records.statement: Erewhon (1872) quotes its fictional treatise as saying that machines' possessing little consciousness now is no security against the ultimate development of mechanical consciousness.

time.note: Title-page year of the 1872 Trübner printing.

records.qualification: Fiction: the narrator quotes the Erewhonian treatise's 'own words'. The passage documents what the novel says, not Butler's view. The dataset records the same passage on B5 as context (ts-b5-erewhon-1872-context). Just before the quoted passage the treatise imagines 'some new phase of mind' unlike any consciousness known; the cross-family check reads mechanical consciousness as a literal mental state that meets U02 (audit F5), with that difference kept. The earlier satirical letter of 1863 (Darwin among the Machines) was located by the cross-family check and is the earliest located U02 articulation; Erewhon is the earliest located novel.

evidence.locator: Chapter XXI, 'The Book of the Machines', p. 191
evidence.passage: There is no security […] against the ultimate development of mechanical consciousness, in the fact of machines possessing little consciousness now.
evidence.note: The omitted words are the narrator's '—to quote his own words—'.
